name: The Turning Stair
goal: Repeat work with loops, and choose between counting, accumulating and searching.

description.what: How to make a program do something more than once: the two loops Python gives you, and the three jobs loops are nearly always doing.
description.why: Everything interesting is repetitive. Without a loop you could only write programs whose length grows with the amount of work they do, so processing a hundred readings would mean writing a hundred lines, and a million would be impossible.
description.enables: Write a program that keeps going until a condition stops being true, that does the same thing to every item in a sequence, and that totals, counts or searches without you knowing in advance how many passes it takes.
description.assumes: You can name a value, work out what an expression evaluates to, and write an `if` with a condition that is either True or False. Nothing else.
description.assessed: You will write loops that run, predict the output of loops written by somebody else, repair a loop that stops one pass too early, and solve problems where nobody tells you which of the three patterns you need.

sections.title: Keep going until: the while loop
sections.body:
Every program so far has run each line once, top to bottom. A **loop** breaks that: it runs the same lines again and again. The first kind is `while`, and it reads exactly as it sounds - while this condition is True, do this again.

A `while` loop has three parts, and leaving any of them out is the classic beginner failure. There is something set up **before** the loop, a **condition** checked before every pass, and something inside the body that **changes** what the condition looks at. The condition is checked first, so a loop whose condition is already False runs zero times - it is not guaranteed to run even once.

If nothing in the body ever makes the condition False, the loop never ends. That is an **infinite loop**, and it does not crash - the program simply sits there, apparently frozen, forever. You spot one by asking a single question of the body: which line moves me closer to the condition being False? If you cannot point at that line, you have written an infinite loop.

Reach for `while` when you do not know in advance how many passes it will take. Halving a number until it reaches 1, reading until somebody types `quit`, guessing until the guess is right: the count is not known when the loop starts, only the stopping condition is.
sections.code:
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("lift-off")

annotations.text: The set-up. The name the condition depends on has to exist, and hold a sensible starting value, before the loop is reached.
The condition is checked HERE, before every pass including the first. If `count` had started at 0 the body would never run at all.
The line that makes the loop finish. Delete it and `count` stays 3 for ever, the condition stays True for ever, and the program prints 3 until you kill it.
Reached only once the condition is False. Execution leaves the loop and carries on down the file as normal.

checkpoint.prompt: Starting from a whole number `n`, you repeatedly subtract 3 until the value is 0 or less. Write `steps_to_zero(n)` returning how many subtractions that takes. `steps_to_zero(10)` is 4, because 10 goes to 7, then 4, then 1, then -2.
checkpoint.starterCode:
def steps_to_zero(n):
    steps = 0
    # keep subtracting while there is still something left
    return steps
checkpoint.hint: The condition is `n > 0`. Two things change on every pass: `n` gets smaller, and the count gets bigger.
checkpoint.explain: The 0 case is the one that catches people: because the condition is tested before the first pass, `steps_to_zero(0)` must give 0, not 1. A loop that always ran once before checking would give the wrong answer here, which is exactly why Python checks first.

sections.title: Do this to each: for and range
sections.body:
The other loop is `for`, and it answers a different question. `while` asks should I go round again?; `for` says here is a run of things, do this to each of them in turn. You do not write the condition and you do not write the update - the `for` handles both, which is why it is much harder to write an accidental infinite loop with one.

`range(n)` produces the whole numbers from 0 up to **but not including** `n`. So `range(3)` gives 0, 1, 2 - three numbers, none of them 3. That is a **half-open** interval: the start is included, the end is not. `range(1, 4)` gives 1, 2, 3, starting where you say and still stopping short of the end.

Half-open looks like a trap and is really a kindness: `range(n)` always produces exactly `n` numbers, and `range(a, b)` always produces exactly `b - a` of them, with no arithmetic for you to get wrong. The cost is the single commonest bug in programming, the **off-by-one error** - you wanted the numbers 1 to 10 and wrote `range(1, 10)`, which stops at 9. To include 10, you write `range(1, 11)`.

A `for` loop is not limited to numbers. `for letter in "cat"` hands you `"c"`, then `"a"`, then `"t"` - one character at a time, in order. Whenever the things you are working through already exist, use `for`; save `while` for when the stopping point is a condition rather than a run of items.

annotations.text: `i` is created by the loop itself and takes a new value on each pass: 0, then 1, then 2. You never assign to it and you never test it.
Two numbers in the brackets means start and stop. This runs 3 times - 4 minus 1 - and the value 4 never appears.
The same `for` over text instead of numbers: `letter` is a one-character piece of text on each pass. Anything Python can hand out one item at a time works here.

checkpoint.prompt:
Exactly what does this print, one value per line?

`for i in range(2, 6):`
`    print(i)`
checkpoint.explain: Four lines, not five: the start 2 is included and the stop 6 is not, so the count is 6 minus 2. Writing 6 on a last line is the off-by-one reflex - the number in the stop position is where the loop halts, never a value it hands you.

sections.title: The three jobs a loop is nearly always doing
sections.body:
Almost every loop you will ever write is one of three shapes. Learning to name them is worth more than learning any syntax, because once you can name what a loop is doing you can write it without thinking about the mechanics.

**Accumulate.** You want one value built out of many. Create the running result before the loop, add to it on every pass, and read it after. The starting value matters and is not always 0: for a running total it is 0, because adding 0 changes nothing; for a running product it must be 1, for exactly the same reason.

**Count.** How many items satisfy some test? This is accumulating by 1 instead of by the item, guarded by an `if`. Start at 0, and add 1 each time the test passes. In the example, `ch in "aeiou"` is a test that asks whether that one character appears anywhere in that piece of text, which is a tidier way to write five `==` comparisons joined by `or`.

**Search.** Which is the first item satisfying some test? Here you want to stop the moment you find it, because the answer cannot change afterwards and because the item you are looking for might be the first out of a million. You also need an answer prepared in advance for the case where nothing matches at all - a search that finds nothing must still hand back something honest, and deciding what that is before you write the loop saves a crash later.

annotations.text: The accumulator, created before the loop. Written inside the loop it would be reset to 0 on every pass and the total would always come out as the last number alone.
The pattern in one line: the new total is the old total plus this item. Nothing here knows or cares how many passes there will be.
Counting is accumulating by 1, and the `if` is what makes it count only the ones you want.
The search answer prepared in advance. If no divisor is ever found, 0 comes out, and 0 is a value no real divisor could be - so the caller can tell the two cases apart.
`break` abandons the loop the instant the answer is known. Without it the loop keeps going and `found` ends up holding the LAST divisor, 17, instead of the first.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `count_odds(n)` returning how many of the whole numbers from 0 up to but not including `n` are odd. `count_odds(10)` is 5, counting 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9.
checkpoint.starterCode:
def count_odds(n):
    count = 0
    # a number is odd when the remainder of dividing it by 2 is 1
    return count
checkpoint.hint: Counting shape: start at 0 before the loop, look at every number `range(n)` gives you, and add 1 to the count when the test passes.
checkpoint.explain: `count_odds(5)` is 2, not 3, because `range(5)` stops at 4 - the odd numbers it contains are 1 and 3 only. Reading the prompt as 1 to n rather than 0 up to n is what produces the wrong answer here, and that misreading is the off-by-one error in its natural habitat.

sections.title: break, continue, and loops that hide their shape
sections.body:
Two words change the flow inside a loop. `break` leaves the loop entirely, straight away, skipping the rest of the body and every remaining pass. `continue` abandons only the current pass and goes back to the top for the next one. `break` ends the loop; `continue` ends the pass.

`break` earns its place in a search, where carrying on after the answer is known is at best waste and at worst wrong. `continue` earns its place as a guard at the top of a long body - skip the items that do not qualify, and everything below is written without an extra level of indentation. That is the whole argument for it, and it is a weak one when the body is three lines: `if n % 3 == 0:` around a short body says the same thing more directly than `if n % 3 != 0: continue` does.

The trap is a loop with several `break` and `continue` statements scattered through it. Every one of them is another way out, and to know what such a loop does you have to hold all of them in your head at once. When you find yourself writing the third one, the loop is usually telling you that it is doing two jobs and wants to be split into two.

`while True:` deserves a special mention: a condition that is never False, made survivable only by a `break` inside it. It is honest when the real stopping test can only be made half-way through the body, and it is an infinite loop waiting to happen if that `break` is ever made unreachable. Write the `break` first, before anything else in the body.

annotations.text: The guard. When the test passes, `continue` sends control back to the top and `print` is never reached on this pass - so only multiples of 3 are printed.
A condition that can never be False. This loop depends entirely on the `break` below it; without one, nothing would ever stop it.
`break` leaves the loop immediately, so `n` keeps the value it had when the test passed - 128, the first power of 2 above 100.
Execution resumes here after the `break`, exactly as if the loop had finished naturally. A `break` leaves the loop, not the program.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `count_until_space(text)` returning how many characters appear before the first space. If there is no space at all, that is the length of the whole text. `count_until_space("hello world")` is 5.
checkpoint.hint: Check for the space before you add to the count, and `break` when you find one. Order matters: adding first would count the space itself.
checkpoint.explain: The text starting with a space separates a correct answer from a nearly-correct one: the `break` has to come before the `count = count + 1`, or the space itself gets counted and every answer is one too high. Same two statements, different order, different program.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `total_up_to(n)` returning the sum of every whole number from 1 to `n` inclusive. `total_up_to(5)` is 15. If `n` is 0, the sum is 0.
guided-practice.hint: This is the accumulator pattern: `total` exists before the loop, grows by `i` on every pass, and is handed back after the loop has finished.
guided-practice.explain: The `n + 1` in the range is what makes `n` itself part of the sum, and the 0 case proves the body never runs when `range(1, 1)` is empty - the answer then comes entirely from the accumulator's starting value, which is why that starting value has to be right.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `count_vowels(text)` returning how many characters of `text` are one of the lower-case vowels a, e, i, o, u. `count_vowels("grimoire")` is 4. Empty text gives 0.
guided-practice.hint: Counting is accumulating by 1 behind an `if`. The test `ch in "aeiou"` is True when that one character appears anywhere in that piece of text.
guided-practice.explain: Counting differs from totalling only in what you add: 1 for each qualifying item rather than the item itself. The empty text shows why the count is created before the loop - with no passes at all there is still an answer to give.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `halvings(n)` returning how many times you can halve the whole number `n` before it reaches 1 or less. Halving throws away any fraction, so 5 halves to 2. `halvings(10)` is 3, because 10 goes to 5, then 2, then 1.
guided-practice.hint: Two things change on every pass: `n` shrinks with `n = n // 2`, and `count` grows by 1. If `n` never changes, the condition never becomes False.
guided-practice.explain: This is a `while` rather than a `for` because nothing knows in advance how many passes it takes - that is the whole reason the question is worth asking. The `n` of 1 case confirms the condition is checked before the first pass, giving 0 rather than 1.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `first_divisor(n)` returning the smallest whole number greater than 1 that divides `n` exactly. `first_divisor(15)` is 3. When nothing below `n` divides it, the answer is `n` itself, so `first_divisor(7)` is 7. You may assume `n` is 2 or more.
guided-practice.hint: Search shape: walk the candidates in order and hand back the very first one that passes the test. Returning from inside the loop stops it as surely as `break` does.
guided-practice.explain: Stopping at the first match is what makes this a search rather than a scan: keep going and you end up holding `n` itself every time, since `n` always divides `n`. Including `n + 1` as the stop is what lets a prime answer with itself instead of falling off the end with nothing.

guided-practice.prompt: `sum_first(n)` should return the sum of the first `n` whole numbers starting from 1, so `sum_first(5)` is 15. It returns 10 instead. Find and fix the fault.
guided-practice.hint: Count the numbers the loop actually visits when `n` is 5. There should be five of them.
guided-practice.explain: `range(1, n)` stops one short, so the answer is always missing exactly the largest term - 15 minus 5 is the 10 you see. The tempting repair is `range(0, n)`, which visits n numbers again and so looks right, but visits the wrong ones: it adds a harmless 0 at the start and still misses `n` at the end.

independent-practice.prompt: Write `digit_sum(n)` returning the sum of the decimal digits of the whole number `n`. `digit_sum(472)` is 13. `digit_sum(0)` is 0. You may assume `n` is 0 or more.
independent-practice.explain: `n % 10` peels off the last digit and `n // 10` removes it, so the number shrinks by one digit per pass and the number of passes is not known in advance. Zero is the case worth checking: the condition fails immediately, no digit is ever peeled, and the answer has to come from the accumulator's starting value.

independent-practice.prompt: Write `smallest_square_over(n)` returning the smallest whole number `k` of 1 or more whose square is strictly greater than `n`. `smallest_square_over(15)` is 4, because 4 times 4 is 16. `smallest_square_over(16)` is 5, because 16 is not strictly greater than 16.
independent-practice.explain: The word strictly is the whole difficulty: with `<` where the comparison needs `<=`, every perfect square gives an answer one too small, and 16 is the case that exposes it. Deciding what the comparison must be before writing the loop is cheaper than discovering it from a failing test.

independent-practice.prompt: A sentence has single spaces between its words and no space at either end. Write `count_words(sentence)` returning how many words it contains. `count_words("the moon is low")` is 4. Empty text contains no words at all.
independent-practice.explain: There is always one more word than there are separators between them - the fence-post problem, four posts and three gaps. Starting the count at 1 handles it, and the empty sentence is the one place that reasoning breaks, since there are no posts at all, so it needs its own answer before the loop begins.

independent-practice.prompt: A prime is a whole number of 2 or more that nothing divides exactly except 1 and itself. Write `is_prime(n)` returning `True` when `n` is prime and `False` when it is not. `is_prime(97)` is `True`, and `is_prime(1)` is `False`.
independent-practice.explain: The answer is False the moment one divisor turns up, and True only once every candidate has been rejected - so the True belongs after the loop, never inside it. Deciding True on the first candidate that fails to divide is the usual wrong answer, and it calls 9 prime because 2 does not divide it.

exam.prompt:
What does this print?

`total = 0`
`for n in range(4):`
`    total = total + n`
`print(total)`
exam.explain: `range(4)` hands out 0, 1, 2, 3 and stops short of 4, so the total is 6 rather than the 10 you would get from 1 through 4. The 0 contributes nothing, which is what makes the mistake easy to miss until the numbers are actually added up.

exam.prompt:
What does this print?

`n = 10`
`while n > 0:`
`    n = n - 4`
`print(n)`
exam.explain: The condition is only checked between passes, never in the middle of one, so the loop overshoots: 10, then 6, then 2, then -2, and only then does the test fail. Answering 2 assumes the loop somehow stops the moment the value would go negative, which nothing in the code does.

exam.prompt: Complete this counter so it returns how many times the letter e appears in `word`.
exam.explain: The three blanks are the three fixed parts of the counting pattern: what you walk through, the increment, and reading the accumulator after the loop. Returning `ch` instead is the classic slip - `ch` exists only to be examined, and holds whatever the last pass happened to leave in it.

exam.prompt: Put these lines in order so the function gives back the first whole number from 2 upwards that divides `n` exactly, or 0 when there is none.
exam.explain: The `return 0` has to sit outside the loop, at the function's own level of indentation: put it inside and the loop gives up after examining a single candidate, reporting nothing found when it has barely looked. The not-found answer belongs after every candidate has been rejected.
The interval is half-open - 3 is included, 9 is not - so the count is simply 9 minus 3. Answering 7 counts both ends, which is the same reflex that produces off-by-one errors everywhere else.

exam.prompt: What does `continue` do when it runs inside a loop?
choices: Leaves the loop entirely and carries on after it
Skips the rest of this pass and starts the next one
Repeats the current pass from the top with the same item
Restarts the loop from its very first item
exam.explain: `continue` ends the pass and `break` ends the loop, so the first option describes the other word. The third is what people fear `continue` means, and it would be an infinite loop, since nothing about the current item would have changed.

exam.prompt:
Trace this loop. Give the value of `total` after each pass through the body.

`total = 1`
`for i in range(1, 5):`
`    total = total * i`

steps.label: after the pass where i is 1
after the pass where i is 2
after the pass where i is 3
after the pass where i is 4

exam.explain: This accumulator starts at 1, not 0, because it multiplies: from 0 every product would stay 0 for ever. Four passes and not five - `range(1, 5)` stops short of 5 - so the answer is 24 rather than the 120 you get by including it.

exam.prompt: A colleague's program freezes and prints nothing when they run it. It contains a `while` loop. Explain what has almost certainly happened, in terms of the loop's condition, and say what has to be true of the loop body for the loop to finish.
exam.explain: A frozen program is not a crash - the loop is running perfectly, it simply has no way to stop, because nothing in the body moves the condition towards being False. The instinct to hunt for a spelling mistake is wrong here: this code is entirely valid, and the fault is in what the body fails to change.

exam.prompt: Write `count_multiples(n, k)` returning how many of the whole numbers from 1 to `n` inclusive divide exactly by `k`. `count_multiples(10, 3)` is 3, counting 3, 6 and 9. You may assume `k` is 1 or more.
exam.hint: Counting shape, with `i % k == 0` as the test.
exam.explain: The `k` of 7 case matters because it never matches: a loop that runs and finds nothing must still give back the accumulator's starting value rather than crash or answer with nothing. The `n` of 0 case proves `range(1, 1)` is empty and the body simply never runs.

exam.prompt: `first_divisor_over(n, m)` should give back the smallest divisor of `n` that is strictly greater than `m`, or 0 if there is none. `first_divisor_over(12, 3)` should be 4, but it answers 12. Find and fix the fault.
exam.hint: The loop finds every match, and each one overwrites the last. Which one do you want to keep?
exam.explain: With nothing to stop it, an assignment inside a loop holds the LAST match rather than the first, which is why 12 comes out instead of 4 - and why the fault hides on any input whose only divisor above `m` happens to be the largest. Walking the candidates downwards instead would answer a different question entirely.
